title: Types of network

stations.name: Standalone computer
facts: A standalone computer works on its own. Its files, software and hardware can only be used on that one machine.
With Wi-Fi off and no cables, the laptop isn't connected to anything, so it is standalone. The others all rely on a network.

questions.q: What is a standalone computer?
questions.a: A computer that is not connected to any other computer or network

questions.q: Which of these is most likely to be standalone?
questions.a: A laptop with Wi-Fi switched off, used to write stories

stations.name: Sharing a file
facts: Email and the cloud both need a network, so without one you have to carry the file on removable media.
Every copy can be edited separately, so it is easy to lose track of which version is the latest.

questions.q: Without a network, how can you get a file onto another computer?
questions.a: Copy it onto removable media, such as a USB stick, and carry it over

questions.q: Two friends pass one essay back and forth on a USB stick. What is the most likely problem?
questions.a: They end up with different versions, and changes get lost

stations.name: Printing
facts: Each standalone computer needs its own printer plugged in, so 30 computers need 30 printers.
More printers means more cost for the machines, ink, paper, electricity and repairs. On a network, one printer can be shared.

questions.q: A room has 30 standalone computers. How many printers are needed so that every computer can print directly?
Why would needing so many printers be a problem for a school?
questions.a: Buying, powering and maintaining lots of printers is expensive

stations.name: Updates and backups
facts: Without a network, someone has to install each update on each computer individually.
There is no network, so there is no server or cloud copy. Without a backup, the files are gone.

questions.q: On standalone computers, how must software updates be installed?
questions.a: Separately on every computer

questions.q: A standalone computer that has never been backed up has a hard drive failure. What happens to its files?
questions.a: They are lost, because there is no other copy

stations.name: Predict
facts: You'll see all four of these in part 2, the school LAN.

questions.q: Match each problem to how a network would solve it.
questions.a: Sharing files → Save files on a file server that every computer can open; Printing → Share one printer between many computers; Installing updates → Install updates on every computer from one place; Backing up → Back up everyone's data centrally, all at once

stations.name: Local area network (LAN)
facts: LAN stands for local area network: small area, one site, and hardware owned by the organisation.
A LAN can use cables, Wi-Fi or both. Connecting to the internet doesn't stop your home network being a LAN.

questions.q: Which best describes a LAN?
questions.a: A network covering a small area, such as one site, where the organisation owns the hardware

questions.q: Is the Wi-Fi network in a home a LAN?
questions.a: Yes: it covers one small site and the household owns the equipment

stations.name: Sharing resources
facts: The file server stores shared files, and the network lets every computer reach them.
Sharing a printer is the benefit. Needing one printer per computer is the standalone problem from part 1.

questions.q: On a school LAN, where are shared files kept so that any computer can open them?
questions.a: On a file server

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a benefit of sharing resources on a LAN?
questions.a: Every computer needs its own printer

stations.name: Advantages
facts: The other three options are all disadvantages of networks.
Central storage on a server means one backup covers everyone's work.

questions.q: Which of these is an advantage of a network?
questions.a: Software can be installed and updated on every computer from one place

questions.q: How does a network make backing up easier?
questions.a: Everyone's data is stored centrally, so it can all be backed up at once

stations.name: Disadvantages
facts: Because the computers are connected, malware on one machine can reach the others.
Up-to-date anti-malware software and security updates stop most malware before it can spread.

questions.q: Which of these is a disadvantage of a network?
questions.a: Viruses and malware can spread from one computer to many

questions.q: Which would best reduce the risk of a virus spreading across a school network?
questions.a: Keep anti-malware software up to date and install security updates

stations.name: The LAN in this room
facts: Every computer's cable runs to the switch, which links them all together.
The file server holds shared files so that any computer on the LAN can open them.

questions.q: In the LAN on this wall, which device connects all the computers together?
questions.a: The switch

questions.q: Which device on this wall stores the files that everyone shares?
questions.a: The file server

stations.name: Wide area network (WAN)
facts: WAN stands for wide area network. It covers towns, countries or the whole world, and joins LANs together.
Size is the key: once a network spans different towns, it is a WAN, even if one organisation runs it.

questions.q: Which best describes a WAN?
questions.a: A network covering a large geographical area that connects LANs together

questions.q: A school trust links the LANs of its schools in different towns. What is this?
questions.a: A WAN, because it covers a large area and joins LANs together

stations.name: Who owns the connections?
facts: Organisations rent WAN links from telecoms companies rather than building their own.
Laying cable over long distances is hugely expensive and needs permission from landowners. Telecoms companies already have the cables in place.
Fibre optic cables on the seabed carry most of the internet's traffic between continents.

questions.q: Who usually owns the connections used by a WAN?
questions.a: Telecoms companies, who rent (lease) them to organisations

questions.q: Why doesn't a school lay its own cable to another school 30 miles away?
questions.a: It would cost far too much and cross land the school doesn't own, so renting a link is cheaper

questions.q: What carries WAN traffic across oceans?
questions.a: Undersea fibre optic cables

stations.name: LAN vs WAN
facts: Now use these to write your three LAN bullet points and three contrasting WAN bullet points in your worksheet.

questions.q: Sort each statement: does it describe a LAN or a WAN?
questions.a: Covers one building or site = LAN; Covers towns, countries or the world = WAN; Hardware is owned by the organisation = LAN; Connections are usually rented from telecoms companies = WAN; Your school network = LAN; The internet = WAN

stations.name: Quick check
facts: The internet is a WAN of millions of connected networks.

questions.q: What is the biggest WAN in the world?
questions.a: The internet

stations.name: Satellite
facts: Satellites cover remote places, but fibre is usually faster and has less delay where it is available.

questions.q: Why are satellites used for some WAN links?
questions.a: To reach places that cables can't easily reach, such as ships at sea

common: Naming a term without saying what it does.
Giving an advantage with no reason attached.
Repeating the question in the answer.
